system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2190-03-19 15:19:00 to 2190-03-21 14:07:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, multiple abdominal surgeries, and recurrent paralytic ileus was admitted for worsening abdominal pain and vomiting over one week. She was managed conservatively with NPO status, NG tube decompression, IV fluids, and electrolyte replacement for hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Imaging showed no bowel obstruction but supported a diagnosis of paralytic ileus, with evidence of slow contrast transit. A possible digestive-genital tract fistula was noted, along with mild metabolic acidosis and venous compression, both of which stabilized during the admission. Urine cultures showed no infection. The patient gradually improved, passing flatus and tolerating oral intake, allowing NG tube removal and discharge home. She was advised to continue supplements, avoid opioids, and follow up with gastroenterology and primary care for ongoing management of Crohn’s, fistula, and mental health concerns including depression and PTSD.

EXAMINATION:  CT ABD AND PELVIS W/O CONTRAST

INDICATION:  ___ with crohn's, multiple surgeries, s/p cholecystectomy,
allergy to IV contrast.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained from the lung bases to the lesser
trochanters after administration of oral contrast only. Coronal and sagittal
reformations were prepared.

DOSE:  DLP: 856 mGy-cm

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS: 

Lungs and Heart: There is very minimal atelectasis is of the right middle
lobe.  The heart and pericardium are normal appearing.

Liver, Gallbladder: The liver is normal in size and attenuation. There are no
focal hepatic mass is identified. The hepatic and portal veins are normal for
and appear patent.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy.

Spleen: The spleen is normal in size and enhancement.

Pancreas: The pancreas shows normal enhancement. There is no pancreatic duct
dilatation or peripancreatic fat stranding.

Kidneys, Adrenals: The kidneys display symmetric nephrograms with no evidence
of hydronephrosis or mass lesion in either kidney.  The ureters are
symmetrical in their course to the bladder.
 The adrenal glands are unremarkable bilaterally.

Bowel:  There is a small hiatal hernia with contrast seen within the distal
esophagus which may the evidence of gastroesophageal reflux. The small bowel
is normal appearing. The patient is status post prior right hemicolectomy. 
The remainder of the large bowel appears normal.

Vessels: There is no aneurysmal dilatation of the abdominal aorta.  The
patient is status post stenting of the right external iliac vein.

Lymph Nodes: There are no pathologically enlarged retroperitoneal or
mesenteric lymph nodes by CT size criteria.

Pelvis: The bladder is unremarkable.  The sigmoid colon and rectum are normal

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks. I’ve been having this pain in my right upper belly for weeks—like a balloon under my ribs. It comes and goes, and now it’s worse. It even goes into my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I vomit every other day, usually after climbing stairs with my grandkids. Not after eating, though. And I’ve had diarrhea for years—had six bowel movements today in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, chest pain, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or breathing issues. But I’ve been really tired lately—barely getting out of bed. My depression’s been worse too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry to hear that. We’ll make sure to address that too. You mentioned past surgeries—can you tell me about those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had about 13 abdominal surgeries—mostly for blockages. I’ve had part of my colon removed, and I don’t have a gallbladder anymore. I also have Crohn’s disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We’ve reviewed your history. You’re also on several medications, including Dilaudid for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 6 mg every six hours as needed. I’ve been on that for a while now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. We’ll continue that for now. You also have a history of PTSD—anything we should know to help you feel more comfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’d prefer not to be alone with male staff if possible. It brings back bad memories from a past hospital experience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll make sure the team is aware and respects that. We’ll always come in as a group when rounding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your CT scan results back. It shows no acute issues—no blockages, gallstones, or pancreatitis. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not clear yet. The pain could be from adhesions or nerve irritation. There’s a small hiatal hernia, which might contribute to reflux, but it doesn’t fully explain your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had hernias before. Could it be blocking something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT didn’t show any obstruction. But we did see a few small gas pockets in your abdominal wall—likely from injections. Nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your sodium was low—127—likely from not eating or drinking much and vomiting. We’re giving IV fluids to correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if not treated, but we caught it early. Your levels are already improving. Your kidney function was a bit off too—creatinine was 1.2, but it’s likely due to dehydration. We expect it to return to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sodium is now 135—much better. Kidney function is improving too. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but not as bad as when I came in. I think it’s closer to my usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We were going to do an MRE to check for adhesions, but it’s not available until later. Since your pain is better, would you prefer to go home and do it as an outpatient?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’d really like to go home. I’m feeling overwhelmed here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll arrange that. We’ll keep you on your regular Dilaudid for pain and continue your other meds, including citalopram for depression and fondaparinux for your vein condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a bit worried about managing the pain at home. Should I take the Dilaudid more often?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, stick to 6 mg every six hours as needed. We’re also giving you a small supply of 2 mg tablets in case you need something milder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the anxiety? Being in the hospital makes it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve prescribed diazepam—just one 5 mg tablet to take before your outpatient MRI if you feel anxious. It should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your morning labs look good. Sodium is 140, creatinine is 0.6—back to normal. Your pain is stable, and you’re alert and walking fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll discharge you. Continue your regular diet—gluten-free as before—and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the MRE?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate with your GI doctor to schedule it soon. Call your PCP or us if the pain worsens or you develop fever, vomiting, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening and helping me get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ve sent instructions to your husband, and follow-up appointments are set. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate everything. I feel much better already.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, multiple abdominal surgeries, short bowel syndrome, and PTSD was admitted for right upper quadrant abdominal pain lasting several weeks, described as a constant pressure radiating to the back, with intermittent vomiting and baseline diarrhea. She also reported worsening fatigue and depression. CT scan showed no acute intra-abdominal pathology, a small hiatal hernia, and subcutaneous gas likely from injections. Admission labs revealed hyponatremia (Na 127) and elevated creatinine (1.2), consistent with pre-renal azotemia from dehydration, which resolved with IV fluids. Pain improved to baseline, and the patient opted to defer MRE for adhesions until outpatient follow-up. She remained on home medications including Dilaudid for pain, citalopram for depression, and fondaparinux for SVC syndrome. Anxiety was managed with scheduled team rounds and a PRN diazepam prescription for future imaging. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged with GI and primary care.
